    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Google’s flagship search experience is evolving into an AI experience with stunning speed.
    • It has been revealed that google search VP Robby Stein confirmed on X that Google is deploying the new desktop search page after a successful test.
    • The search button has obviously been a part of Google’s search page forever.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Google’s flagship search experience is evolving into an AI experience with stunning speed. Even time-tested elements of search are getting AI makeovers, and the latest to get this treatment is the search homepage on Google.com. A redesign that’s been in testing for the last few weeks is now official, bringing easier access to AI chats and dropping the dedicated search button entirely.

    It has been revealed that google search VP Robby Stein confirmed on X that Google is deploying the new desktop search page after a successful test. The page will now have a few more buttons under the search bar, all connected to AI features. There’s an image generation button, one for analyzing files, and one for brainstorming with Gemini. The “I’m Feeling Lucky” button remains, but the Google Search button that used to sit next to it is gone.

    The search button has obviously been a part of Google’s search page forever. However, it wasn’t in a very convenient location in the modern interface. When you begin typing a query, the autocomplete suggestions cover that button. You have to click out of the text field to access the button, which is an extra step compared to simply mashing the Enter key to run your search.

    Recent findings suggest that the other massive change brings your recent AI conversations to the forefront. If you’re logged into Google, the search homepage will have an expandable sidebar on the left with your recent AI Mode search threads. This sidebar will also be accessible on the results page. According to Stein, the sidebar made a “big difference” in how people made progress on their web searches, calling it a “simpler way to pick up where you left off.”.

    It’s easy to feel frustrated by changes like this if you don’t like Google’s new AI approach to search. But at the same time, the loss of functionality is minimal. Google probably has usage data that highlights that particular search button was rarely used. Most people probably just hit Enter or click an autocomplete suggestion to go to the results.

    Industry observers note that this change states more about Google’s priorities and the future of search. AI features get prominent buttons, and your AI conversations now have a whole sidebar UI. Meanwhile, traditional search is increasingly de-emphasized. There may come a day when AI Mode takes over completely, forcing you to manually select the old-fashioned version of search. It does feel like Google is inching in that direction.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Relatives of the missing victims flocked to the factory’s entrance, seeking updates about their loved ones.

    A fire at a confectionery factory west of Jakarta has killed three people with 36 remaining missing, an Indonesian rescue official notes.

    Drone footage highlighted large parts of the factory destroyed, with the roof collapsed in places and smoke still rising from the complex. Photos and videos shared by rescuers show officers entering the charred building in search of the missing victims on Sunday, with small fires still burning in some spots.

    Relatives of the missing victims flocked near the factory’s entrance, seeking updates about their loved ones, footage aired by local broadcasters indicated.

    The Fonusa Agung Mulia factory, located in Cikande in Indonesia’s Banten province about 50km from the capital, caught fire on Saturday afternoon, search and rescue official Rizky Dwianto said on Sunday.

    “All elements of the joint SAR [search-and-rescue] team are making maximum effort to locate the victims while prioritising the safety of personnel in the field,” he added.

    Rizky remarked four people were injured and taken to a nearby hospital and health clinic.

    Firefighters were alerted about 4.30pm on Saturday and found the building already engulfed in flames when they arrived, fire official Tubagus Machfudz told local broadcaster Kompas TV.

    “When we arrived … a large area was already on fire. So we could not determine whether the company’s protection system was functioning properly or not,” he remarked.

    The Banten province governor Andra Soni told reporters overnight that an estimated 60 people were inside the factory when it caught fire.

    The cause of the incident is still under investigation, the local disaster agency said in an Instagram post on Sunday.

    Deadly fires are not uncommon in Indonesia.

    In December last year, a blaze that was likely caused by a drone battery explosion tore through a seven-storey building in Jakarta and killed at least 22 people, police remarked.

    In 2023, at least 13 people were killed in the country’s east after an explosion at a nickel-processing plant.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Spotify founder Daniel Ek is backing Europa Fusion, a stealthy fusion power startup founded by an AI researcher who is taking a different approach to developing a fusion power plant.
    • The U.K.-based startup was founded in February, though sources told TechCrunch that the founder, Nantas Nardelli, has been working on the idea for longer.
    • Nardelli has extensive experience in the AI world, having previously worked at Google DeepMind, Facebook AI Research, and Microsoft Research Cambridge.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Spotify founder Daniel Ek is backing Europa Fusion, a stealthy fusion power startup founded by an AI researcher who is taking a different approach to developing a fusion power plant.

    The U.K.-based startup was founded in February, though sources told TechCrunch that the founder, Nantas Nardelli, has been working on the idea for longer. The people asked not to be identified because the information isn’t public. Bloomberg first reported Ek’s backing of Europa Fusion.

    Nardelli has extensive experience in the AI world, having previously worked at Google DeepMind, Facebook AI Research, and Microsoft Research Cambridge. Recently, he was head of machine learning at Pacific Fusion, the fusion power startup based in Fremont, California.

    In a recent development, pacific Fusion recently broke ground on a demonstration facility in New Mexico. Like most fusion startups of its size, Pacific Fusion leans heavily on physical devices to test its theories and improve its simulations.

    Nardelli apparently didn’t agree with the focus on hardware, instead thinking that fusion startups should invest in a more simulation- and data-heavy approach, a source familiar with his thinking told TechCrunch.

    It has been revealed that like Pacific Fusion, Europa Fusion will pursue a pulsed-power approach to fusion. Pulsed-power reactors use massive, perfectly timed surges of electrical current to compress fuel targets until the atoms inside fuse and release energy.

    According to recent reports, fusion power has the potential to be a significant energy source in the coming decades, but to date, no one has built a power plant capable of supplying electricity to the grid. If fusion power becomes commercially viable, though, it could possibly be a significant source of carbon-free power that draws on nearly limitless fuel supplies. The technology also has the potential to alleviate concerns about AI’s energy consumption.

    Fusion’s ability to generate electricity without exacerbating climate change apparently drove Nardelli’s pivot from AI.

    Recent findings suggest that “My original background is in electronics and control engineering,” he wrote on his website. “I used to build robots for a living. One day I’ll be back to that, but it’s time to fix climate change for good.”.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • George Washington died in 1799 after serving for two terms as America's first president.
    • A framed lock of hair from America's first president, George Washington, has been sold at auction for $4,000 (Â£3,058).
    • The hair once belonged to John Gadsby, who entertained Washington in 1799 just before the latter's death the same year, and was later obtained by a collector called John K Lattimer from a descendent of Gadsby's, according to Richmond Auctions, which sold the item.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    George Washington died in 1799 after serving for two terms as America's first president.

    A framed lock of hair from America's first president, George Washington, has been sold at auction for $4,000 (Â£3,058).

    The hair once belonged to John Gadsby, who entertained Washington in 1799 just before the latter's death the same year, and was later obtained by a collector called John K Lattimer from a descendent of Gadsby's, according to Richmond Auctions, which sold the item.

    Its new owner has not been named.

    Saturday's sale is not the most expensive for Washington hair at auction. Three strands thought to have been removed from him close to or after his death stored in a locket sold for nearly $40,000 in 2021.

    Gadsby, a resident of what in 1799 was the town of Alexandria in Virginia, entertained Washington for dinner shortly before his death later that year, according to a testament given in 1928 by Gadsby's granddaughter, Julia Ten Eyck McBlair, and which was posted on the Richmond Auctions website.

    McBlair stated that her grandfather came into possession of Washington's hair "in view of the friendship and association with his last days" and had it framed and hung "under General Washington's portrait in our home in Washington City, there I have seen it all my life".

    Gadsby hosted Washington's two birthday celebrations in 1798 and 1799, Richmond Auctions states.

    Sources indicate that washington led American forces to victory against the British in the War of Independence and helped draft the US Constitution before becoming the country's first president in 1788. He stepped down in 1797 after serving two terms.

    Several locks of Washington's hair have been preserved, including at least 50 examples that are in a collection at his former residence, Mount Vernon, which is now a museum.

    "Public displays of hair from friends or loved ones peaked in the 19th century, but had long been popular among affluent families like the Washingtons," a blog on the Mount Vernon website states.

    As well as lockets of his hair, other items associated with Washington have also done well at auction.

    In July, a signed letter by Washington from 1776, in which he asks for soldiers for the Continental Army to fight the British, sold for $109,800.

    Race to be next UN secretary general exposes divisions among world powers

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Debate about dominance of permanent five members could reignite if major powers block Costa Rican frontrunner.
    • Sources indicate that the race to become the next UN secretary general could reach a decisive moment on Friday when a UN security council vote is likely to reveal whether the Costa Rican frontrunner for the post would be blocked by the substantial powers.
    • In a recent development, rebeca Grynspan, an economist and UN insider who is from a family of Polish-Jewish wartime refugees to Costa Rica, has been in the lead in all but one of the eight straw polls of the 15 UN security council members since the first secret ballot was held on 30 July.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Debate about dominance of permanent five members could reignite if major powers block Costa Rican frontrunner.

    Sources indicate that the race to become the next UN secretary general could reach a decisive moment on Friday when a UN security council vote is likely to reveal whether the Costa Rican frontrunner for the post would be blocked by the substantial powers. If so, the setback will reignite a debate about the dominance of the permanent five (P5) members at the United Nations.

    In a recent development, rebeca Grynspan, an economist and UN insider who is from a family of Polish-Jewish wartime refugees to Costa Rica, has been in the lead in all but one of the eight straw polls of the 15 UN security council members since the first secret ballot was held on 30 July. Each member goes down the list of candidates, casting an “encourage”, “discourage” or “no opinion” vote for each candidate.

    It has been revealed that despite countries not being required to reveal how they voted, it is thought Grynspan’s candidature has been resisted by Russia and the US, two of the five permanent security council members that can ultimately wield a veto against a candidate. Knowledge among the security council delegations of how countries are voting is down to private intelligence, leaks and a process of elimination.

    The intensive lobbying over the job has spread across the globe, but Friday is especially important since the poll is slated to differentiate the voting of the P5 from the 10 elected members (E10) of the security council. To be recommended as secretary general to the UN general assembly, a candidate needs nine votes and no vetoes. In Friday’s colour-coded secret ballot, the P5 will cast red ballots and the E10 white.

    One diplomat mentioned: “The electoral system means it is important how many votes you win, but equally how many of certain votes you don’t lose.”.

    The protracted 140-day deadlock confirms the polarisation that has hampered the incumbent secretary general, António Guterres, but also belies claims the role is now an irrelevance.

    Friday’s secret ballot may also reveal whether the United Arab Emirates’ campaign for its diplomat, Lana Nusseibeh, is about to blow up in its face due to the hostility to the UAE’s brand of active, commercially driven diplomacy, not just in Sudan, but also Somalia, Western Sahara, Libya and Yemen.

    Sources indicate that A late entrant, in the two straw polls in which she has contested so far, Nusseibeh secured only seven “encourage” votes, six “discourage” and two “no opinions”. This is despite prestigious major-power backing and her acknowledged personal diplomatic skills.

    It has been revealed that nusseibeh has US and Russian backing. The French foreign ministry may have misgivings about the UAE, but Emmanuel Macron, the French president, travelled to the UAE in the midst of French riots to see the UAE president, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, and secure 100,000 metric tons of diesel a month.

    According to recent reports, in the UK, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has kept his counsel, but he shares a Polish-Jewish refugee heritage with Grynspan and cannot be an admirer of the UAE’s human rights record or its evasion of EU sanctions on Russia. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has UAE connections from his time as mayor of Manchester, and Nusseibeh is a fellow alumnus of the University of Cambridge. At the UN she worked closely with the UK in an informal group called “Friends of the Future of the UN”.

    Yet 68 British MPs, including the Labour chair of the international development select committee, Sarah Champion, last week signed a letter calling on Burnham to veto Nusseibeh, describing her as “a tainted and compromised figure”.

    Sources indicate that some of the opposition to her from elected security council members is not wholly political. Latin American countries believe an informal rotation system means it is their turn to lead the UN. As a result Panama and Colombia, right now on the security council, will oppose her. China has also been supportive of this rotation principle.

    In a recent development, but others deeply object to what they consider to be the UAE’s dollar diplomacy and preparedness to use its extraordinary wealth to exacerbate and exploit pre-existing divisions in a country to gain a commercial foothold. Somalia, for instance, has a seat on the Security Council, and its president, Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, this week went on TV to accuse the UAE of buying ports, establishing military bases and supporting armed forces outside Somalia’s national security framework without federal approval.

    It is also possible that Finland and Latvia, the two elected members with the greatest stake in Ukraine, are unimpressed that the UAE gave Vladimir Putin red carpet treatment when he visited Abu Dhabi in December 2023, nine months after the international criminal court had issued an arrest warrant for child trafficking. Greece, less engaged in Ukraine, may be more flexible.

    Sources indicate that since the last poll, Nusseibeh has been to Bahrain, Britain and Pakistan, a clue as to where extra votes may be harvested. She also had a “thoughtful exchange” with Zeng Jixin, the Chinese ambassador to the UAE.

    In a recent development, the two hurdles are whether someone so deep inside the UAE inner circle would have the courage in office to show true independence, and whether her active denials of UAE involvement in arming the RSF in Sudan leave her irretrievably tainted. From a Palestinian intellectual family, she insists she would make peace in Sudan her number one priority.

    In the last ballot on 5 November, Grynspan won 12 votes in favour and three negative. But on 16 October – the only colour-coded ballot so far – which distinguishes between permanent and elected members – she received two discourage votes from permanent members, the equivalent of a veto. Nusseibeh had not joined the race at that point.

    In an administration as personalised as the US, it has been hard for Grynspan to gain influence, with many sensing that Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, is the key influencer.

    It has been revealed that grynspan has been reluctant to make the fact she is Jewish a feature of her candidacy, but the election of a Jewish person to run the UN might be seen as something the US could embrace as transformative. Her age – she is 70 – could be considered a drawback among those calling for a younger generation to renew the institution.

    According to recent reports, although there are other Latin American candidates, Grynspan is seen as a more viable candidate than her rival, the Argentine Rafael Grossi, the head of the UN weapons inspectorate. Russia has opposed Grossi, objecting to his interventions over the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant in Ukraine.

    One way or the other, the logjam has to be broken soon.

    The Xiaomi 18 Pro proves two screens aren’t better than one

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1273 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: The Verge

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The rear display isn’t good for much, but these are great phones in almost every other respect.
    • The rear display isn’t good for much, but these are great phones in almost every other respect.
    • If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The rear display isn’t good for much, but these are great phones in almost every other respect.

    The rear display isn’t good for much, but these are great phones in almost every other respect.

    If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

    Industry observers note that xiaomi introduced a second screen to its flagship phones with last year’s 17 Pros, but didn’t release them outside China. That means the newly introduced 18 Pro and Pro Max are the first chance I’ve had to find out if a screen on the back of a phone is any more useful now than it was when Xiaomi last tried it on 2021’s Mi 11 Ultra — not to mention earlier efforts by the likes of Nubia and Vivo.

    According to recent reports, after a week or two with both of Xiaomi’s fresh Pro phones, I’m not entirely sold. The rear display has a single, obvious use case — it’s helped me take some of the best selfies I’ve ever managed — but it isn’t very useful otherwise.

    According to recent reports, the rest of the phones are great, with good cameras, major batteries, and a more flexible take on the privacy display seen in the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra. There’s a lot to like. But with prices higher than ever thanks to the RAM crisis, it’s hard not to wonder how much buyers are paying for a second screen they could probably do without.

    Excellent main and telephoto camerasPrivacy displayStrong performanceCompact.

    Rear display is limitedBasic ultrawide cameraExpensive.

    Excellent main and telephoto camerasPrivacy displayStrong performanceExtended dynamic range.

    Rear display is limitedBasic ultrawide cameraExpensive.

    Industry observers note that there are two Xiaomi 18 Pro phones: the £1,199 Pro (around $1,570) and the £1,399 Pro Max (around $1,830). In the UK and Europe, they’re priced to compete directly with the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max.

    It has been revealed that they come in similar sizes to the iPhones, too: a 6.4-inch display on the Pro, and 6.9 inches on the Pro Max. There are a few other differences, though not many. The Pro Max’s 7,050mAh battery is bigger than the Pro’s 6,000mAh (with larger batteries available outside Europe), and its 100W wired charging is 10W faster too. Both phones last a day pretty comfortably and will stretch to two with lighter use, though only just — I’ve seen better battery life from recent Oppo and Vivo flagships. They also use Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 chips, though only the Pro Max has the Extreme version. And while the camera setups are nearly identical, you’ll get slightly better dynamic range from the bigger phone thanks to a LOFIC sensor.

    Industry observers note that the rear screens also vary slightly in size between the phones, though at either 2.7 or 2.9 inches, there’s not much in it. Wrapping around the two main rear camera lenses, they look a lot like the displays you’ll find on the front of foldables like the Galaxy Z Flip 8, though smaller than most of those, and much more limited in functionality.

    Industry observers note that you can set your choice of wallpapers, some of which are interactive. Listen to music or a podcast, and playback controls appear. You can turn on notifications, useful for when you want to rest your phone face down, but Xiaomi’s implementation is odd: App icons appear so large on the screen that there’s no space to fit much text from a given notification; there are no interactive responses like quick replies or marking emails as read; and you can’t see a list of your notifications, only viewing each for a few seconds as it comes in. It makes this just barely more useful than a notification LED.

    In a recent development, unlike flip phones, you can’t use the small screen to access the phone’s settings, and you certainly can’t run full-blown apps. Instead, there’s a natural-language AI tool to create your own apps, powered by Google’s Gemini 4 Argon. It’s good for simple tools or games — I made a pomodoro timer and a semi-functional knockoff Pac-Man — but your creations can’t connect to the internet or access other apps, so anything you make will be quite purposefully limited.

    Industry observers note that the only thing that’s convinced me the rear screen is at all worthwhile is its camera viewfinder. The UI’s a little fiddly at this scale, but you can take photos, record videos, or create a photo booth-inspired picture set, all using the rear main camera. I’ve taken the best selfies of my life with this phone, which may be reason enough for some people to buy it.

    It helps that the main camera is especially good. It and the telephoto are both excellent 200-megapixel shooters with large sensors, capable of great results in almost any lighting conditions. The telephoto’s short minimum focusing distance of 12cm lets it double as a great macro camera too. The 18 Pro Max has a slight photographic advantage, with a LOFIC main sensor that offers an expanded 16-stop dynamic range, helping it capture better highlights in particularly tricky lighting. Most of the time you won’t see a huge difference between the two phones.

    In a recent development, xiaomi’s longtime camera partner Leica is involved again, and by default you can shoot in one of two Leica-branded camera modes — Vibrant or Authentic — plus a fresh third option, the Xiaomi-branded Original, which splits the difference between them. The other big Leica contribution is a new Essential Moments mode that uses AI to simulate three different retro Leica aesthetics in either 35mm or 75mm lenses.

    The ultrawide, set apart from the other two lenses beneath the screen, looks like an afterthought — and it shoots like one too. It’s placed so low on the body that my finger frequently blocks its view; its 17mm focal length barely feels wider than the 23mm main camera, so it doesn’t give you much extra room to play with; and its smaller sensor means quality is noticeably worse than from either of the other rear cameras, especially in dimmer light. As for the selfie camera, it’s decent, but you’ll only ever use it for video calls since the rear screen makes the main camera the better choice the rest of the time.

    Industry observers note that the Xiaomi 18 Pro phones have one other trick: a privacy display. This is a pretty direct imitation of Samsung’s Galaxy S26 Ultra tech, switching between different sets of pixels with varying viewing angles to make your screen hard to see from the side when it’s activated. Like Samsung’s version, you can turn it on across the phone or just for certain apps; unlike Samsung’s, when you activate it for specific apps, it also applies to specific notifications, and it works with split-screen or floating windows without affecting other apps open at the same time. It’s more flexible than Samsung’s version, though to my eye, less effective.

    According to recent reports, the Xiaomi 18 Pro and Pro Max have plenty of strengths, with great main and telephoto cameras, good performance, and reasonably attractive designs. But shortcomings like the lackluster ultrawide camera and batteries that don’t last as long as some rival flagships make me wonder about the compromises made to fit that rear display. Its limited functionality has given me pause, especially as flagship phones like this hit increasingly eye-watering prices.

    The representative in the US House expected to chair the House Intelligence Committee in January, Jim Himes (D-Conn.), has threatened to withhold support for funding government-owned systems from SpaceX amid the ongoing inquiry into the use of Starshield in Ukraine.

    According to recent reports, “SpaceX’s potentially unilateral modification of a U.S. Government contract, combined with its lack of responsiveness to congressional oversight, calls into question every contract the U.S. Government has with SpaceX,” Himes wrote in a letter to SpaceX founder Elon Musk on Friday.

    CNN first reported the letter’s existence. The network also reported that Himes sent a classified communication to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton with a similar message that it would be difficult for Congress to authorize funding for systems with SpaceX as the primary vendor.

    It has been revealed that spaceX has developed the consumer Starlink service over the last decade, which provides high-speed Internet from low-Earth orbit to user terminals on Earth. For government customers, SpaceX has also developed Starshield, a suite of satellite services that includes a militarized version of Starlink communications. The US government has purchased Starshield services and extended access to Ukraine, although the terms governing that access are largely classified.

    During the last several weeks, a controversy has erupted over interruptions to Starshield service in parts of Ukraine, cutting off connectivity to drones used to defend against Russian attacks.

    On October 19, for example, Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy noted of Starshield on social media, “Unfortunately, we have established that the equipment stops functioning at speeds of 130–161 kilometers per hour in various sectors of the front. This is slowing down our frontline logistics and limiting the use of various types of drones, particularly mid-strike drones and interceptors of jet-powered ‘shaheds.’” Additional disruptions were reported a week ago.

    Recent findings suggest that the central question is who decided to curtail the performance of Starshield assets in Ukraine. Accounts have variously implicated Musk, SpaceX, the Pentagon, and the White House. Musk has mentioned that US officials control Starshield access, while defending SpaceX’s right to restrict the use of commercial Starlink service in war.

    In a recent development, “My ask to you is straightforward,” Himes wrote to Musk. “Explain the changes that were made to the Starshield service in October 2026, why those changes were made, and whether those changes were made unilaterally by SpaceX or were directed by a U.S. Government official.”.

    The communications from Himes suggest that Congressional Democrats, who will control the House and Senate in January following decisive victories in the Midterm elections, are prepared to not just investigate the disruption of these SpaceX services in Ukraine, but to take action that could threaten SpaceX’s broader national security business.

    “It is difficult for me to continue supporting the authorization of funding for these SpaceX-developed, government-owned systems, until I receive satisfactory answers to my questions about the Starshield service in Ukraine,” Himes wrote in his letter to Musk.

    It has been revealed that various options are open to Congressional Democrats, as well as some Republicans who have raised similar concerns, including demanding classified briefings and documents and restricting funding through appropriations to the US Department of Defense and other federal departments. Notably, the US Space Force awarded SpaceX a $2.29 billion contract earlier this year to develop the Space Data Network Backbone intended to support the Golden Dome missile defense initiative. That program, along with SpaceX’s work building intelligence satellites for the National Reconnaissance Office, could become a focus of congressional scrutiny.

    It seems unlikely that the US government would sever ties with SpaceX for space-based data services or rolls out, as the organization is at the moment providing capabilities that no other US company can match. But Democrats are clearly serious about putting restrictions on Musk’s ability to influence geopolitical conflicts that have traditionally been the purview of governments rather than corporations.

    In a recent development, the arrests took place at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport around 8 a.m. local time (1600 UTC) on Saturday. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) stated the operation targeted Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, a Mexican national who had overstayed his visa.

    #93059. Experts warn: Nearly everyone in AI is susceptible to a honey-trap scheme right now

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (926 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

    Experts warn: Nearly everyone in AI is susceptible to a honey-trap scheme right now

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (926 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Even as the fall-out for Nvidia over Jensen Huang’s alleged honey-trap scandal is still unfolding, Silicon Valley has yet to reckon with a fresh reality: many more people among them are at risk.
    • “Nobody briefs founders on counterintelligence,” Aaron Brown, a former senior CIA officer and current founder of the software company Lumbra, told TechCrunch.
    • That’s because historically honey traps have been associated with politicians, the military, and national intelligence — the people “behind clearances and a workforce trained to expect an approach,” from spies and other attackers.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Even as the fall-out for Nvidia over Jensen Huang’s alleged honey-trap scandal is still unfolding, Silicon Valley has yet to reckon with a fresh reality: many more people among them are at risk.

    “Nobody briefs founders on counterintelligence,” Aaron Brown, a former senior CIA officer and current founder of the software company Lumbra, told TechCrunch.

    That’s because historically honey traps have been associated with politicians, the military, and national intelligence — the people “behind clearances and a workforce trained to expect an approach,” from spies and other attackers.

    Recent findings suggest that but now many of the most valuable secrets “sit inside companies building chips, models, and infrastructure,” Brown indicates, adding that a spy “wants what the CEO can touch. The roadmap, the export decisions, the customer list, who gets the technology. The CEO is the shortest path to all of it.”.

    Huang has been accused of falling for just such a honey trap by having an affair with Alice Huang. She’s a former executive of a Singapore neocloud who’s been accused of being a Chinese spy and of smuggling billions of dollars’ worth of restricted Nvidia chips into China.

    Industry observers note that after the Huang allegations broke, jokes flooded the internet about which tech CEO will be next, but it’s not just CEOs and founders who are at risk. The WSJ reported that OpenAI started warning its employees about outsiders trying to cozy up to them in search of company secrets. Anyone with access to sensitive information — from board members to executive assistants — can be the target of a honey trap.

    Recent findings suggest that and typically, the attackers aren’t lovers. Friendship is actually the oldest honey-trap scheme around, Brown stated.

    Honey traps gain access to their targets as investors, customers, recruiters, and consultancies. Their requests look legitimate on paper and don’t need their targets to fall in love. “They need you to feel comfortable talking,” Brown remarked. “They last longer because nobody’s looking.”.

    Sources indicate that what’s interesting, too, is the irony. So many tech founders are moving to automate and digitize so much of human life and yet remain vulnerable to the oldest bug around, a person who preys on the human need to be understood by others.

    “Why fight through a firewall when you can get close to the person who can open doors, influence decisions, or make requests nobody wants to question?” Perry Carpenter, a criminologist and chief deception strategist at KnowBe4, told TechCrunch.

    Once targets realize they have been compromised, the threat can escalate: attackers now have a means of blackmail.

    Sources indicate that another irony: AI has made honey-trapping much easier and cheaper. Planning a scheme used to take months or years of research, crafting a persona, knowing the target, and executing a strategy. These days, it’s easy to use AI to research a target, generate fake social profiles, fake backgrounds, even fake voice calls.

    Industry observers note that “AI can help sustain an entire fictional backstory,” Carpenter said. “The technology helps set the stage, but the deception ultimately plays out through human relationships.”.

    The AI industry “became a national security industry faster than its culture caught up,” Brown noted.

    “Part of being honey-trapped is not knowing,” he added. “It doesn’t feel like manipulation. It feels genuine, even lucky.”.

    According to recent reports, carpenter stated a good first step is looking for unusual patterns. Note, for instance, “coincidental encounters that happen a little too often,” he said. There are also obvious signs, like persistent curiosity about work and colleagues, or requesting secrecy about meeting up, and pressing for introductions or information.

    Industry observers note that bigger red flags include if someone’s requests are getting bigger, pushing the boundaries of what you usually would be uncomfortable doing. “A simple gut check,” Brown said. “Would this person still be around if you lost your job tomorrow?”.

    According to recent reports, it also helps to try and understand when emotions might be influencing a decision. Carpenter suggests putting up a clear boundary between one’s personal and professional life. Within companies, it also helps to “eliminate executive exceptionalism,” he said, the idea that the rules don’t apply to people in power at the company.

    Brown added that company culture plays another role, too: Are employees comfortable with raising concerns, challenging unusual requests, and escalating possible threats? “One of the most dangerous security cultures is one where nobody feels comfortable questioning the CEO,” Carpenter noted.

    “Founders need to take risks, and they need to explore business opportunities,” Brown said. “Paranoia doesn’t help. Recognizing you’re a target does.”.

    #93057. Latest Update: ‘Weak and dizzy’: the secretive ICE force-feeding tactics that ended a Cuban father’s hunger strike

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2530 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theguardian ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: ‘Weak and dizzy’: the secretive ICE force-feeding tactics that ended a Cuban father’s hunger strike

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2530 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Exclusive: Luis Alejandro Cora Pérez says in messages to Guardian from inside Texas facility pain of force-feeding caused him to break strike.
    • According to recent reports, the text message that came from inside the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention center was stark: “I have spent five days eating regular food.
    • A Cuban asylum seeker, Luis Alejandro Cora Pérez, 32, said in messages to the Guardian this month that he was still weak and dizzy after three months without eating, but that he had broken his hunger strike because being force-fed was just too painful.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Exclusive: Luis Alejandro Cora Pérez says in messages to Guardian from inside Texas facility pain of force-feeding caused him to break strike.

    According to recent reports, the text message that came from inside the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention center was stark: “I have spent five days eating regular food. If I don’t eat it, they put the tube in me to feed me.”.

    A Cuban asylum seeker, Luis Alejandro Cora Pérez, 32, said in messages to the Guardian this month that he was still weak and dizzy after three months without eating, but that he had broken his hunger strike because being force-fed was just too painful.

    The Trump administration responded to requests for comment by denying it had force-fed Cora Pérez. But the detainee sent more details – and his is far from an isolated case.

    Cora Pérez was one of two men on hunger striker at a Texas facility for whom ICE sought and received a federal judge’s permission to force-feed in recent weeks, a Guardian investigation found.

    Cora Pérez and the other man were locked up inside the Port Isabel service processing center, an ICE detention facility in south Texas, just a few miles from the US-Mexico border, on the coast near where Elon Musk’s SpaceX releases rockets. Cora Pérez began a hunger strike in August to protest against his prolonged detention by federal immigration officials while his case plays out. At first he only drank water, then after three weeks, he says he began to drink one Ensure nutritional shake per day.

    On 30 October, court records show ICE received permission to forcibly feed and hydrate him, and to restrain him while doing so.

    The next day he claims six guards at the center held him down, while medical staffers inserted a feeding tube through his nose and down his throat, and pumped nutritional liquid into his stomach – a process he called “traumatizing, both physically and psychologically”.

    On 3 November, ICE then received permission from a federal judge to force-feed another hunger striker at Port Isabel, from Uzbekistan, federal court records show. The DHS says the Uzbek man has not been subjected to the practice, however.

    On Wednesday night, after weeks of communications, Cora Pérez was suddenly transferred to another detention center in Texas. His relative says neither of them were alerted to any plans to transfer him, or a reason for it.

    The DHS did not specify why Cora Pérez was transferred, adding that ICE makes custody determinations on a “case-by-case” basis based on “various factors”.

    The revelations come as ICE’s detention practices continue to come under fire amid allegations of mistreatment, and as an increasing number of sporadic hunger strikes have been breaking out in ICE facilities across the country.

    The two men’s cases in Texas, revealed here for the first time, are some of the most recent instances of government lawyers seeking a federal judge’s permission, as required by ICE policy, and receiving the go-ahead to force-feed detained hunger strikers. The Guardian’s reporting is based on court records, interviews, dozens of messages exchanged and an interview conducted with Cora Pérez via a facility phone. It further reveals how the Trump administration is increasingly obtaining such court orders to force-feed detained immigrants, a secretive practice widely condemned as torture by human rights organizations and medical ethics groups.

    Detainees driven to hunger strike are typically using it as a last resort to protest against poor conditions and the Trump administration’s preference for arrest and prolonged detention while their civil immigration cases proceed through the system.

    In a recent development, cora Pérez remarked detention center staff inserted the feeding tube and left it in his body, a not uncommon practice, according to experts, and introduced nutrition – first a “clear liquid”, followed by a “milky liquid”, he recalled – through the tube twice more that day, before he cracked and said he broke his hunger strike, citing what he called “horrific torture”. He began voluntarily drinking nutritional shakes the following day, he said.

    “ICE does not hold back on anything, and they do anything they want, like we have seen, even killing their own US citizens,” he wrote to the Guardian, referring to the fatal shootings of Renee Good by an ICE officer and Alex Pretti by a border patrol officer in January of this year during Trump’s pivotal immigration crackdown on Minneapolis.

    Industry observers note that detained hunger strikers subjected to involuntary medical procedures, including force-feeding, have rarely spoken out about their cases or revealed their identities, much less while still detained. Cora Pérez’s messages offer a rare glimpse at conditions inside a detention center’s restricted medical unit where hunger strikers and suicidal detainees are held.

    “They just took [the Uzbek man] in an ambulance after [him] fainting in front of the medical lobby where they take our vitals, our weight and our temperature,” Cora Pérez said in an alarmed message last Monday morning.

    The Uzbek man was returned the following day to the facility, Cora Pérez noted.

    “I see him every day because I see him in the room in front of me, but they don’t let us talk to each other,” he added.

    The Guardian independently confirmed the Uzbek’s man identity but is not publicly naming him, because efforts to contact him have been unsuccessful. The man arrived at the Mexico-US border in April 2022 and was released into the country while navigating his immigration case. He was arrested by border patrol officials in April of this year and placed in detention. The man does not appear to have any criminal record and the DHS did not point to any criminal history.

    In a statement, DHS noted that after they received the court’s permission to force-feed the Uzbek man, he “has voluntarily taken in fluids and there has been NO force-feeding or forced hydration”.

    Security operations at the sprawling Port Isabel facility in Los Fresnos, Texas, are run by a private prison organization, Akima Global Services, while healthcare is primarily handled by government workers.

    In a recent development, “ICE respects detainees’ rights to exercise self-expression and medical autonomy by refusing nourishment and medical care,” the DHS stated in a statement. “ICE Health Services Corps may provide involuntary medical treatment only to prevent imminent life-threatening harm or death. Medical staff may provide treatment only to medically stabilize the patient, bringing the detainee outside the imminent harm, incapacitation, or death.”.

    The US attorney’s office in the southern district of Texas, which represented ICE in its force-feeding request, did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Virginia-headquartered Akima Global Services, and its parent firm Nana Regional Corporation, based in Alaska, did not respond to a request for comment.

    Force-feeding cases are shrouded in secrecy. After a detainee launches a hunger strike, ICE often sequesters them in medical isolation cells for monitoring, according to ICE’s detention standards. The DHS mentioned that ICE continues to offer hunger strikers three meals per day.

    Sources indicate that after a certain period of not eating, which varies per case, ICE will request a federal judge’s permission to force-feed the hunger striker. Many court records, and sometimes entire court dockets, are sealed and hidden from public view. In Cora Pérez and the Uzbek man’s cases, like in others, they did not have any legal representation to challenge the force-feeding requests.

    Industry observers note that the Guardian found at least five instances in which ICE requested permission to force-feed hunger strikers in Port Isabel since January 2025. The federal judge who ruled on Cora Perez and the Uzbek man, Rolando Olvera, has similarly ordered in at least three other cases, records show. Olvera’s judicial assistant said the court had no comment for this article.

    ICE is known to have requested permission to force-feed at least 21 detainees across the US since January 2025, the Guardian found, but the number is probably higher since an unknown number of records and dockets remain sealed, unsearchable and not feasible to locate. Most of the cases coinciding with the second Trump administration and tracked by the Guardian are in Texas and Florida, with others in Georgia, Arizona and Washington state. Under the Biden administration, ICE force-feeding requests were also made in Louisiana and California.

    Amy Zeidan, an emergency medicine physician based in Atlanta and an expert on healthcare in immigration detention, remarked force-feeding hunger strikers can amount to “torture”, and lead to significant psychological distress. She also said it was a violation of medical ethics.

    Sources indicate that “Essentially it’s like inserting a straw into your nose,” Zeidan mentioned. “You have a gag reflex, so most times people will gag, and that’s really uncomfortable. And people will even vomit repeatedly if it continues to irritate their gag reflex.”.

    Zeidan added that the forceful insertion of a feeding tube can lead to the swelling of the nostrils and the throat, and even tear them, leading to bleeding.

    “It is like torture – somebody is doing a painful procedure to you that you don’t consent to,” Zeidan added. “Autonomy is a fundamental principle of medical ethics. We can’t do something to patients if they don’t want to, even if we think it’s good for them.”.

    Industry observers note that there are numerous cells and rooms inside the Port Isabel medical unit, including isolation cells and shared rooms for ill detainees, according to Cora Pérez. In recent weeks, there were five people in the Port Isabel medical isolation cells used for hunger striking or suicidal detainees, he added. He described the cells as “practically freezing”, constantly surveilled with a security camera, and with just a bed, toilet and sink. As well as himself, he indicates he observed the Uzbek man, a Middle Eastern man, a “tall” eastern European man and a Black man of unknown nationality in the isolation cells. Unit detainees are escorted by facility staff to showers and sometimes receive yard and television access, he noted.

    Cora Pérez worries for the other detainees. The Black man, whose identity or nationality he does not know, seems to have “serious mental health problems”, Cora Pérez observed.

    “He harms himself and spends the night yelling and hitting the door, and does not let anyone sleep,” he said.

    The Guardian has independently confirmed the eastern European and Middle Eastern men’s identities, but is not publicly naming them because efforts to contact them have been unsuccessful. The DHS did not comment on the other men inside the medical isolation unit, saying they could not comment without the Guardian providing their identities.

    Cora Pérez had left his son and parents in Cuba and requested asylum at the Mexico-US border in 2023, according to a relative who spoke to the Guardian on condition of anonymity due to fear of retaliation by immigration authorities. Cora Pérez went to live with the relative in Florida, where he worked in maintenance at a hotel and as a food delivery worker, he stated.

    In March 2025, Cora Pérez was arrested by local police and later convicted of two misdemeanors, including “breach of peace” and “obstructing an officer without violence”, according to local records. He was sentenced to two months in jail, his relative stated. But ICE placed a hold on him and as he was being released in June 2025, immigration officials took him into custody – a common system – and soon transferred him to the Adelanto detention center, a privately-run facility in California.

    Sources indicate that days in Adelanto turned to weeks, then months, then over a year, according to a federal court order denying one of his petitions requesting his release. His multiple requests to immigration and ordinary federal courts for release from detention, while he fights his asylum case, have been unsuccessful.

    In a recent development, “All his claims will be heard by an immigration judge, and he will receive due process. This administration will not ignore the rule of law,” DHS remarked. “Criminal illegal aliens are not welcome in the US.”.

    In August, he stopped eating to protest against his protracted detention.

    According to recent reports, “I have spent two birthdays behind ICE’s bars,” he wrote. “The reasons I did the hunger strike in Adelanto are for my political asylum, for the time I have spent detained, [and] because I have a 14-year-old son who is starving to death in Cuba because he does not have my help.

    “Also due to the mistreatment by the officials,” he added.

    Sources indicate that cora Pérez did not tell his family about the hunger strike, so as not to further worry them. It was not until he was transferred to Port Isabel in late September that he confessed to his relative he had been on a prolonged hunger strike.

    “He doesn’t share details so that I won’t get upset or worry,” the relative mentioned in a phone interview.

    Cora Pérez’s mother, who is in Cuba, “does not know anything, because she is sick, and with his detention she has gotten worse”, the relative added, between tears. “I don’t want her nor his grandmother to know anything about it,” the relative added.

    On 30 October, the federal prosecutors requested permission for ICE to forcibly feed and hydrate Cora Pérez. Hours later, a federal judge approved the procedures without hearing from Cora Pérez. Cora Pérez told the Guardian in various instances he felt it was unfair he was not given the opportunity to present his case to the judge before the judge approved his force-feeding.

    Industry observers note that “It’s very disturbing because the judge is basically making a decision on information that is only provided by one side,” said Linus Chan, a professor of clinical law and the director of the detainee rights clinic at the University of Minnesota law school. “That just seems ridiculous.”.

    Cora Pérez was force-fed the following day, he said in his messages and in a phone call, adding that he did not physically resist because he “had seen a lot of mistreatment of others detained”.

    It has been revealed that “[ICE does] what they want with us, whatever they want, because a federal judge gave them permission,” he added. “I have suffered on the island [of Cuba] and now at the hands of ICE.”.

    Industry observers note that after asking Cora Pérez about the DHS’s denials that he was force-fed, he repeated that he was. “Brother, ICE says and does whatever they want. They deny, punish, retaliate and do everything at their own will. They have even sent Cubans to Africa,” he mentioned.

    In a recent development, the number of people detained by ICE has soared under the Trump administration. And due to policy and legal changes, tens of thousands of people are forced to stay in detention for long periods while they fight their immigration cases.

    Chan, from the University of Minnesota, states prolonged detention and delays in their cases lead to logical conclusion. “That’s exactly when people protest,” he said.

    “And the only form of protest, for many of these people, is a hunger strike,” he stated.

    As Trump’s hardline immigration crackdown continues and people are detained as a first resort while their cases play out, Chan stated: “Hunger strikes will become more common.”.

    Homes along Los Angeles' Sunset Boulevard could be seen engulfed in flames during the fires of January 2025.

    A jury in Los Angeles has found a 30-year-old man guilty of starting one of the most destructive wildfires in California's history.

    Jonathan Rinderknecht was convicted of arson after starting the fires that swept through Pacific Palisades and parts of Malibu in January last year, killing 12 people and destroying more than 6,800 buildings in the US state.

    The conviction was handed down nearly five months after deadlocked jurors led to the judge declaring a mistrial.

    Sources indicate that rinderknecht, who had pleaded not guilty, was convicted of two federal charges. He is due to be sentenced on 17 March when he faces between five and 20 years in prison on each charge.

    Jonathan Rinderknecht's arrest in October last year.

    Rinderknecht was found guilty of lighting a fire on 1 January last year which burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up six days later.

    One of the charges was for starting the original brush fire, while the other centred on the damage caused when it reignited into a catastrophic blaze.

    "We were determined to hold him accountable, and today's guilty verdict delivers a measure of justice for the families who lost loved ones and the thousands whose lives were upended," stated Bill Essayli, who leads the US Attorney's Office for the Central District of California.

    Rinderknecht is a Los Angeles resident and former ride-share delivery driver.

    Defence attorney Steve Haney had argued at trial that prosecutors lacked sufficient physical evidence or records to prove their case.

    Lawyers for the defendant said they were "disappointed" by the verdict but respected the jury's decision.

    Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, who was widely criticised for her handling of the fires, stated in a statement that "no verdict can bring back the lives lost or erase the pain families have endured".

    "So many are still struggling to rebuild," she noted. "For those still displaced, the devastation remains a daily reality.".

    Prosecutors had argued that Rinderknecht was driven by revenge, anger and loneliness because he had nowhere to go for the holiday.

    They cited geolocation data from his iPhone, security camera footage that indicated his car's location and witness testimony from passengers.

    They alleged that Rinderknecht had a "deeply entrenched belief that the wealthy were destroying the world" and in turn purposely started the blaze in the affluent neighbourhood.

    The fire was one of several that ignited back-to-back across the LA region in January, which in total left 31 people dead and destroyed 16,000 structures.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • AI changed the game at Chess.com, helping it expand to 11 other classics this year.﻿.
    • AI changed the game at Chess.com, helping it expand to 11 other classics this year.﻿.
    • According to recent reports, if you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    AI changed the game at Chess.com, helping it expand to 11 other classics this year.﻿.

    AI changed the game at Chess.com, helping it expand to 11 other classics this year.﻿.

    According to recent reports, if you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

    Chess.com is ready to go a lot bigger than chess. After launching Gambit, a gambling-free poker site, earlier this year, the firm is now adding 10 more games: backgammon, checkers, go, hearts, mahjong, shogi, sudoku, solitaire, xiangqi, and a Scrabble alternative called word. They’re all part of Chess’s new Classic Games platform, which is launching its public beta on Saturday on the web and through a new app for iOS and Android.

    “Our cofounders have had many people come up to them and say, ‘Hey, I run a mahjong night on Wednesdays’ or ‘I go to this local bar in Chicago with like five people, and we love playing go, but we lack a Chess.com,’” chief growth officer Albert Cheng notes in an interview with The Verge. “The way that Chess.com has grown this community of almost 300 million members has not really happened for a lot of these other types of classic games.”.

    Classic Games is aimed at filling that gap. Some of the newly introduced games, like shoji or xiangqi, are strategy games similar to chess while others are further afield, like sudoku, solitaire, and word. The Classic team chose the new games through “a mix of community feedback, market research, and then just our own confidence in our ability to serve that game well,” Cheng notes. It’s focused on classics that “have some sort of lifelong journey of learning and a community.”.

    Classic Games will feel familiar if you’ve ever played a match on Chess.com. Each game has lessons, leaderboards, and a rating system. Multiplayer games like checkers or mahjong have options for matches against other players or bots, and they use the same bot characters that Chess.com has. (Martin remains the lowest-rated bot across the board, whether it’s on Chess, Gambit, or Classic.) Not all of the games have the same play modes — word and mahjong have puzzles like chess, while sudoku has a set of daily grids and solitaire has daily deals.

    In a recent development, the expansion hasn’t put Chess.com itself on the back burner, according to Cheng. If anything, it’s never been better. “Chess is more and more so in the public zeitgeist than I’ve ever seen it, frankly, during my time here,” Cheng says. “Our daily active consumers are higher than they’ve ever been during the firm’s history.” He declined to share exactly how many daily users Chess.com currently has but remarked the site is “doing amazingly well.”.

    So, while the company is expanding beyond its domain name, chess remains its primary focus. “The amount of folks that are fully dedicated toward building fresh games is less than 1 percent of the company,” according to Cheng.

    AI played a key role in helping Chess.com launch 11 upcoming games in a matter of months with a team of only a few people. Earlier this year, Cheng told The Verge his team built Gambit with the help of AI, mainly for coding tasks. He claims they used “almost entirely the same approach” for Classic, with AI helping to speed up the coding process again.

    “Because these games are built on top of the Chess.com code base and design system and bot characters and rating systems, it’s a huge advantage and allows us to move very promptly alongside AI to bring these types of games to market with a very small team,” Cheng notes. “As we create more and more games, the adjacent games that can be created to it just happen much faster because the infrastructure is there, as opposed to standing everything up from scratch.”.

    AI wasn’t used for Classic Games’ art and design, Cheng says. “The look and feel of it is very carefully crafted by humans, and we’re proud of that,” he says. “The truth is, it really is a blend. It’s a small team of really talented folks that have good product and design judgment, and they’re leveraging AI.”.

    “We are fortunate in some ways that AI and chess have been intermixed for 30-ish years.”.

    Chess.com’s comfort with AI may come from the fact that human chess players have now spent decades playing and learning alongside machines. “We are fortunate in some ways that AI and chess have been intermixed for 30-ish years,” Cheng states, calling back to Garry Kasparov’s 1996 chess match against IBM’s Deep Blue supercomputer. “Even before the organization was founded 20 years ago, the idea that AI was super powerful at the game of chess was embedded in how the cofounders thought about the company.”.

    According to recent reports, elsewhere in the games industry, there’s been increasing tension over the use of AI. Cheng says that while Chess.com may be using AI to “accelerate” coding tasks, the creative side of things has become more notable. “On the art and the design side, the ratios are shifting a decent amount, where we’re hiring more of those folks,” he says, adding that the company has “shipped a lot more major features in Chess.com than in previous years” using what they’ve learned from Classic Games’ faster development process.

    Chess.com might not be done growing its library of games, either. Cheng said it will likely expand to “a lot more” games in the future.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Apple is being sued in India by a U.S.-based startup that alleges the iPhone maker’s NameDrop feature, which lets people share contact information by bringing devices close together, infringes its patented technology.
    • GG Technologies, the startup behind StayTouch, an app that lets users exchange contact details by bringing their phones close together, is seeking ₹15 billion (about $161.86 million) in damages and an injunction against Apple, per court documents reviewed by TechCrunch.
    • Santa Monica-headquartered GG Technologies filed the lawsuit in India in October after mediation proceedings initiated in April failed in September, the startup told TechCrunch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Apple is being sued in India by a U.S.-based startup that alleges the iPhone maker’s NameDrop feature, which lets people share contact information by bringing devices close together, infringes its patented technology.

    GG Technologies, the startup behind StayTouch, an app that lets users exchange contact details by bringing their phones close together, is seeking ₹15 billion (about $161.86 million) in damages and an injunction against Apple, per court documents reviewed by TechCrunch.

    Santa Monica-headquartered GG Technologies filed the lawsuit in India in October after mediation proceedings initiated in April failed in September, the startup told TechCrunch. Pre-institution mediation is generally required before filing commercial lawsuits in India. The company also sued Apple in the U.S. in April over related patent infringement claims.

    Sources indicate that in its 781-page court filing in the Bombay High Court, GG Technologies alleged that Apple’s NameDrop infringes its Indian patent on technology that helps phones exchange contact details with nearby devices without requiring manual pairing. The organization released StayTouch in 2019, the same year it first sought patent protection for the technology in the U.S. It filed its Indian patent application in 2021 and received the patent in July 2024.

    Industry observers note that apple introduced NameDrop as part of iOS 17 in June 2023. The feature debuted on iPhones later that year, with support for compatible Apple Watches arriving in October through watchOS 10.1.

    “We are seeking an injunction to restrict the usage of the NameDrop feature which is native to iOS,” GG Technologies told TechCrunch. GG Technologies urged the court in its filing to restrict Apple from selling or importing iPhones and Apple Watches preloaded with NameDrop in India. The case has yet to be listed for a hearing.

    In the U.S., the International Trade Commission opened an investigation into Apple’s alleged patent infringement in August, following a complaint from GG Technologies. The startup is seeking an order that could block imports of infringing Apple devices into the country, along with restrictions on their sale.

    Sources indicate that founded in 2018 by Gaurav Goel, a graduate of the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Delhi and a former Goldman Sachs investment banker, GG Technologies developed StayTouch as an alternative to exchanging business cards. The app is available on iOS and Android.

    Apple did not respond to a request for comment.

    According to recent reports, india has become increasingly important to Apple, both as a fast-growing consumer market and a major manufacturing hub outside China. The Cupertino firm has expanded its retail presence in the South Asian nation, where iPhones still account for less than 10% of smartphone shipments, giving considerable room for growth.

    #93047. Trump FCC declares California isn't allowed to enforce phone service rules

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (744 w)
    📖 Baca
    Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

    Trump FCC declares California isn't allowed to enforce phone service rules

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (744 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Federal Communications Commission ordered California to stop enforcing its Carrier of Last Resort (COLR) rules against AT&T, setting up another battle between the Trump administration and California over the state’s right to enforce its own telecom laws and regulations.
    • Industry observers note that AT&T’s status as a Carrier of Last Resort in California requires it to offer telephone service to any potential customer in its territory.
    • Recent findings suggest that the order released today granted AT&T’s request to preempt state rules, following up on the FCC’s previous approval of AT&T’s petition to discontinue service.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Federal Communications Commission ordered California to stop enforcing its Carrier of Last Resort (COLR) rules against AT&T, setting up another battle between the Trump administration and California over the state’s right to enforce its own telecom laws and regulations.

    Industry observers note that AT&T’s status as a Carrier of Last Resort in California requires it to offer telephone service to any potential customer in its territory. AT&T wants to stop offering basic phone service to newly introduced customers and discontinue service for 184,000 residential customers and 15,000 business customers on June 1, 2027.

    Recent findings suggest that the order released today granted AT&T’s request to preempt state rules, following up on the FCC’s previous approval of AT&T’s petition to discontinue service. AT&T had tried to achieve the same result in court, but a federal judge rejected its request to override California’s rules in July.

    The FCC order probably isn’t the last word, as California could sue the commission. California has stood alone against AT&T, which has received relief from COLR obligations in 20 of the 21 states in its wireline service territory.

    Recent findings suggest that “California’s Carrier of Last Resort framework may have made sense when it was established 30 years ago,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr stated in a statement released with today’s order. “But those rules were designed for a bygone era and no longer make sense in today’s competitive, advanced marketplace.”.

    Industry observers note that if AT&T ends service on its old copper lines, many homes and businesses would not be offered modern fiber networks. AT&T claims a wireless home phone service that connects to the cellular network will be good enough, and the FCC agreed.

    It has been revealed that “The FCC has granted AT&T’s applications to replace legacy voice service with a modern, IP-based alternative in certain areas of the state. California’s state requirements are blocking AT&T from proceeding with a federally authorized transition,” Carr noted.

    In a recent development, california notes its rules allow wireless replacements if they meet the state’s standards for basic phone service, but that AT&T must demonstrate that its wireless phone service would meet the COLR obligations. California’s requirements include flat-rate options for unlimited voice calls, discounted Lifeline rates for eligible low-income customers, and telephone relay service for people who are deaf and hard of hearing.

    In a recent development, FCC Democrat Anna Gomez voted against the order, saying that state telecom commissions “are often the last line of defense for consumers. They know their communities, they take their complaints, and they answer to the people who rely on these services in a way that a federal agency in Washington cannot always match.”.

    Recent findings suggest that gomez said the California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) has an open proceeding on how to modernize its COLR rules, and that the FCC should let that process play out. Large technology transitions work best “when the state regulator is a partner with a real role,” but the FCC is treating the CPUC “as an obstacle to be cleared,” she said.

    The CPUC “proceeding is the right place for California to weigh what a modern basic service requirement should look like, with input from the people who will actually be making that switch,” Gomez noted. “AT&T has said it does not initiative to discontinue service before June 1, 2027, which leaves time for the CPUC to finish its work. Rather than wait, this item tells the CPUC to write its new consumer protections around a federal ruling it opposed.”.

    In March, the FCC issued an order that made it easier for carriers to discontinue copper networks. The order asserted that state rules are subject to preemption if they conflict with the FCC’s discontinuance authorizations and authority. AT&T cited the order in its lawsuit against California.

    Trump officials and telecom companies have been trying to block California’s rules for years. The first Trump administration lost an attempt to preempt state net neutrality laws throughout the country in 2019, and California later defeated ISPs in a lawsuit that challenged its net neutrality law in court.

    According to recent reports, california’s net neutrality law and other telecom regulations are again being threatened by rules the Trump administration applied to federal grants, but California rejected US demands to stop enforcing its laws this month. In that case, California may have to choose between enforcing its telecom laws and receiving $1.42 billion to deploy broadband to 270,571 locations.
